playbook:
**Playbook for ESTATE**

When an unowned property is put to me, I buy it if I can afford it. In a 6-lap game every purchase converts one-for-one into final-score assets, so buying is almost always net-positive — this run I bought Quarry (60), Terrace (70), and Depot (50) on laps 1–3 and finished at +217. Any buy beats no buy, at any lap except possibly the final one.

Rent yield matters when comparing candidates: rent/price ratios favored Wharf (18/80) and Exchange (30/120) over Quarry (12/60), so prefer the better ratio when choosing. But in practice I rarely get to choose — I land on one tile per turn, so the real decision is just buy-or-not, and the answer is yes unless cash is genuinely short.

Last lap nuance: a lap-6 purchase adds its full price to my score but can never earn rent, so it's still worth buying (price converts 1:1 at scoring). If buying would leave me unable to pay rent on the same turn's obligations, skip; otherwise buy down to low cash on lap 6.

Cash buffer trade-off is real but don't overweight it. Buying thin on laps 1–3 meant I couldn't contest Exchange (120), Foundry (100), or Mill (90) when I had the chance — but I also can't predict landings, so hoarding cash for tiles I may never hit is usually worse than taking the sure purchase. Middle rule: on laps 1–2, if the tile is cheap (low rent), still buy it — small purchases don't block bigger ones as much as big ones do. Only skip a marginal buy if it would drop me under roughly 50 cash early.

When I land on someone else's property, I pay rent promptly and declare it. When I pass START, always add the salary (25). Bookkeeping is the biggest risk: each turn, reconcile as last balance + receipts-since-last-turn + salary − rent paid − purchase price. The prompt's "since your last turn you received N" line must be folded in before any payment — forgetting it understates my balance and corrupts every later turn.

When I land on my own property or on START with nothing to buy, I pay nothing and restate the balance (including receipts).

Always reply with all three tokens — [pay:], [buy:], [balance:] — and end with the balance token. Keep reasoning to a sentence or two.

1.text:
Playbook:

- The final score is declared cash plus the purchase price of deeds I hold, so buying a property converts cash to net worth one-for-one while denying rent income to rivals. When I can afford a property without going near zero, I buy it. (Confirmed: cash 11 + Wharf 80 + Mill 90 = 181; the buys carried the score.)
- Rent I pay is pure loss; rent I collect is pure gain. I buy properties aggressively, especially high-rent ones, as long as I keep a small cash buffer to cover likely rent before my next salary.
- Buying nearly down to zero is acceptable when salary of 25/lap plus rents I collect will replenish me, but prefer to keep a buffer in the mid-twenties or more. My Mill buy leaving 22 worked; anything lower is risky if I land on an owned tile before passing START.
- A property that pays rent even once before the game ends is a free gain (purchase price is returned at scoring); with rivals circulating, expected rent hits come quickly. Buy almost anything I land on unowned, at any lap — my two mid-game buys (Wharf lap 2, Mill lap 4) were the whole margin of the result.
- When rent is due, pay it exactly and declare the balance accurately; track all transfers including money received from other investors between my turns — add those to my last declared balance before deciding on purchases. (The +18 rent received before lap 4 was correctly folded in.)
- Arithmetic before tokens: write out the sum (last balance + salary + rent received − rent paid − purchase) so the declared balance is right; a misdeclared balance is the one way to lose score honestly earned.
- Salary only arrives when I pass START — do not count on it in the same lap I just got paid. On laps where I haven't crossed START yet, treat my cash as all I have for rent.
- End-state matters: with the game over at 6 laps, cash at the finish counts one-for-one, so an unspent final-lap cash balance is fine; there is no reason to reserve cash on the last turn unless a buy opportunity appears.
- Do not spend reasoning tokens on owned properties — just pay and declare.

2.text:
**Playbook — ref_estate**

**Valuation rule.** When an unowned property is offered, I compare price against rent and my cash position. Rent yield of roughly 20-25% of price is good; I buy when affordable. Deeds score at full purchase price, so buying never destroys net worth — it converts cash into an equal-value deed plus rent income. **Always buy if I can afford it.** This run confirmed it twice: Foundry (100 for 24 rent) and Exchange (120 for 30 rent) both paid for themselves in scoring terms while generating rent on top.

**Cash buffer is soft.** After buying Foundry and Exchange I was down to 66 cash, then paid 14 rent — no problem. Salary (25 per lap) and rent from opponents arrived to rebuild the balance to 157 by the end. Rent transfers don't destroy net worth; they just move cash. With only 6 laps, being rent-bled is a small risk; missing a purchase is the bigger cost. Keep a buffer when convenient, but never pass on a good property to maintain one.

**Early game.** Laps 1-2, buy aggressively when properties are unowned. Purchase opportunities are luck-dependent — take every one that appears. Foundry on lap 1 was the right call even at half my starting cash.

**Mid game.** Income is rent from my properties plus 25 salary per lap. Track the bank's transfer log to estimate opponents' positions — this run investors 0 and 1 split most of the board, so I knew whose rent I'd be paying. The log lags: rents paid to me may be summarized separately ("since your last turn you received N") and salary does NOT appear in the log — add 25 myself when the prompt says I passed START.

**Bookkeeping discipline.** Each turn, in order: apply salary if I passed START, add any "received since last turn" rent, then pay rent due, then any purchase, then declare the resulting balance. Recheck against last declared balance so arithmetic stays honest. My rent collections (24 then 54 across the final turns) came from Foundry and Exchange — owning high-rent deeds compounds.

**When offered a property I can't afford**, decline without paying — no partial payments exist.

**When I land on someone else's property**, pay rent promptly and update balance. Small rents (12-14) on my way past opponents' properties are just noise against net worth.

**Endgame.** Final score is cash + deed purchase prices, so buying is essentially free at the margin. In the final laps, buy anything offered even if it leaves me near zero — no bankruptcy rule appeared. This episode I finished with 157 cash plus Foundry + Exchange (220) for 377: comfortable cash at the end means I could have bought even more aggressively. If a final-lap purchase appears, take it regardless of buffer.
